norms.what: The skill runs as a slash command with an optional path. Asking about scope before any work costs a round trip on the one decision a user rarely wants to make; stating the assumption in the report keeps it visible and correctable.

These are the surfaces Claude Code reads instructions from: the memory files and their `@path` imports, path-scoped rules, subagent definitions, skills, commands and settings. API code is included because four of the Opus 5.5 breaking changes live in request code rather than in prose.

`rg` skips hidden entries while traversing, so a sweep from `.` walks past `.claude/`, where most of a Claude Code setup lives, and exits 0 with zero hits, which reads as a clean audit. Naming the directory, or passing `--hidden`, is what makes the search reach it.

Instruction trees are often materialised by a tool — a plugin install, a sync script, a shared package — and gitignored in the project that receives them. An edit there is silently discarded by the next install, or, through a symlink, changes another project. Reporting the change for its source keeps it from being lost.

A mature setup can hold hundreds of instruction files. Reading all of them at once fills the context window and dilutes attention on each file, which is where an audit loses findings. Measuring first costs one command and decides everything after it. Bytes divided by four is a deliberately rough estimate: it only has to size batches, not bill anyone.

The batch ceiling keeps each audited slice small beside a 1M-token window, so the pattern table and the batch both sit in focus. Grouping by relationship keeps an import and the file importing it in the same view, which is where a contradiction between them shows.
A long audit that says nothing reads as stuck. A one-line statement of intent before the work starts is the update cadence the Opus 5.5 guide recommends for human-in-the-loop runs.

Writing findings to disk after each batch turns the audit into a sequence of small, focused passes whose results survive context compaction, and lets the report be built from the file rather than from memory of earlier batches.

One line per finding with a location, a pattern id and a quote is what the report groups and counts, and what a later re-scan compares against. A dated path keeps a second audit from overwriting the first.

Several rows apply only to one kind of project — chat, unattended agents, API code. Recording a row's signal where its condition does not hold produces findings the user has to argue away, which is the fastest way to make an audit unreadable.

The skill was narrowed to one transition so that every proposed change rests on one guide. Verification steps, delegation prompts and severity filters became outdated with Opus 5, not 5.5; they are still worth knowing about, so they are listed, and left to an audit whose evidence covers them.

A model upgrade changes how instructions about model behavior land; it changes nothing about a project's facts or its safety boundaries. An audit that removes a confirmation step because it looks redundant does real damage, so those classes are protected by rule rather than by judgment.
A large setup produces more findings than a chat message holds. A file keeps the whole report reviewable, shareable and diffable, and gives Stage 5 a place to record what was applied.

Where the session can publish a page, a report is easier to read and to share with a team there than in a file inside the repository. It is conditional because the tool exists only in some Claude environments.
The chat summary exists to support the decision in Stage 4, not to replace the report.

The first version proposed a full diff in the report. A diff for every finding is expensive to produce and mostly discarded once the user chooses a subset, so it is written only for what was approved.

Which changes to make is the user's decision. A question with options is answered in one step, where a list of decisions inside a long report has to be found first. The recommendation is bounded so the skill never recommends applying a change the guide does not state.
Headless runs (`claude -p`, CI) have no interactive question tool. Changing nothing there keeps an unattended run from editing a project without approval.
Mixing an audit's edits into uncommitted work makes both hard to review and impossible to revert separately.

The approval covers a specific set of changes. Applying more than that, even an obviously good change, turns the approval into a blank check. Files marked read-only in Stage 1 are reported for their source instead, per [N04].
One of the Stage 4 options is to review the diff first; this norm is what makes that option mean something.
An edit can leave a pattern in place — a removed sentence repeated elsewhere in the same file — or remove more than intended. The re-scan checks both, against the same table the audit used.

The Opus 5.5 guide recommends testing several effort levels against the project's own evals rather than carrying settings over. The audit applies documented guidance; only the project's measurements show it holds for that project.
A report that records only findings cannot answer, a month later, which of them were acted on.
